@internal Emitted once by a cloud worker that accepts the turn_handoff control request, after it registers, carrying what it wrote to external_metadata.turn_handoff: the version, the tools whose calls it would accept, the worker life (worker_epoch) announcing it, whether handed-off calls wait for files still being staged (staged_files), whether user messages that make no model call are appended before a handed-off turn (no_query_first), whether two assistant messages of a turn may share a message id (shared_message_id), whether a turn_handoff request may name a rewind it depends on (requires_rewind_request_id), and relay_marker, home_files, file_names, carried_writes and hydrates_carried_lines when set. Lets a session client learn the capability from the event stream instead of reading worker state. Durable in the stream: a reader keeps the entry with the newest worker_epoch it has seen and ignores older ones; a worker life that does not accept turn_handoff emits nothing (its registration writes turn_handoff: null).

@internal Emitted when a previously-yielded message is superseded or removed from the transcript (e.g., streaming→non-streaming fallback removes a partial orphan). Consumers that render or persist the stream should remove the referenced message. From internal QueryEvent 'tombstone'.

@internal Emitted when tool execution adds/removes tool_use ids from the mid-execution set (after permission grant, before result). Surfaces use this to show which tools are running. From internal QueryEvent 'set_in_progress_tool_use_ids'.

@internal Emitted while compaction is running (hook phase, compact start, compact end). Distinct from system/compact_boundary, which reports the post-compaction transcript boundary after completion. From internal QueryEvent 'compact_progress' (CompactEvent Delta-track arm).
@internal Entries not installed: event not forwarded by this worker, unknown kind, malformed, or duplicate id.

@internal Epoch milliseconds on the sender's clock when this request was issued — informational only: a device client judges staleness by how long the delivery waited on the session service's clock (the age its stream stamps on the event) against deadline_ms, never by this value against its own clock, and answers a stale delivery fail-safe (a guard answers 'retry') rather than leaving it unanswered. Optional and additive on the public hook_callback wire; hosts that do not know it ignore it.

@internal Epoch milliseconds on the sender's clock — kept on the wire but informational only: the serving client judges lateness by how long the delivery waited on the session service's clock (the age its stream stamps on the event) against deadline_ms, never by issued_at on its own clock, and answers a late or undatable leg refused 'stale' — nothing runs — instead of leaving it unanswered. A durable catch-up into a fresh client still never runs an old call; the age check refuses it.
@internal Every other hook not sent: on an event that is not forwarded, a duplicate of one already listed, or beyond a cap.

@internal Fate of a queued command (slash command or queued user prompt). 'queued' when the inbound message enters the command queue; 'started' when it drains into a turn; then exactly one terminal state: 'completed' — the turn that consumed it ended cleanly; 'cancelled' — removed by cancel_async_message (the host's own, or — with Remote Control enabled (remote_control) — a remote client withdrawing a prompt that a remote client queued: such a uuid was never sent by the host, so there is nothing to resend and the frame is informational), swept by an interrupt with cancel_queued:true or, in a remote session and behind a flag, by a plain interrupt, which cancels only messages that the server had sent again (see `cancelled` on the interrupt's response), caught by a pending cancel just before dispatch, or consumed into a turn that was aborted (interrupt) or died on a hard failure (model_error, prompt_too_long, ...) — cancelled-over-completed is deliberate dup-over-loss for exactly-once resenders, so a fold answered earlier in a failed turn may be re-sent (a per-fold ledger refinement is tracked separately) — but resenders must not blindly resend on 'cancelled': user-requested removals arrive as the same state, so correlate against your own cancel_async_message responses AND against any interrupt receipt's `cancelled` list (interrupt_cancel_queued_v1) and resend only cancels neither source accounts for; 'discarded' — the session ended (end_session) with the command still queued, or with a peer message still held by the receive-side policy (not preceded by 'queued' then); 'refused' — declined by the session's receive-side policy before entering the queue (outright, or after being held): not preceded by 'queued', and it will not run in this session. Known gap: folds consumed by turns ending via max_turns / hook_stopped / tool_deferred / background_requested report 'completed' even though their content may only be answered on continuation/resume. A prompt sent with requeue_if_interrupted_within_ms that an interrupt puts back reports 'queued' again (after its 'started', if that was reported), then goes on as any queued prompt does. 'completed' means the consuming turn ended, not that the result frame was delivered. Ordering relative to the result frame is per-path: a command that starts a fresh turn emits 'completed' AFTER that turn's result frame (later still when the result is held back for background tasks); a command folded into an already-in-flight turn emits 'completed' BEFORE that turn's result frame. Not a strict pairing: a terminal state may arrive for a command_uuid that never emitted 'started' (control-request ACKs, duplicate deliveries); internally-enqueued commands (cron triggers, teammate shutdown prompts, deferred-turn resume) mint a fresh uuid at enqueue and emit started/terminal without 'queued'; a turn that fails by throwing can leave 'started' without a terminal state; and a peer message the queue's own admission guard drops after acceptance (rate limit, duplicate collapse, loop guard, queued-peer cap) currently leaves 'queued' without a terminal state — on process exit a wrapper should synthesize 'discarded' for uuids it has not seen reach a terminal state. The exactly-one-terminal guarantee is per worker process, not per uuid lifetime: after CCR redelivery a 'discarded' uuid legitimately re-emits queued→…→terminal on the next worker. Emitted on the stdout stream in -p/SDK sessions; remote transports (mobile/desktop bridge) receive the equivalent signal via delivery ACKs instead. A host driving a cloud-hosted session through the headless `--cloud` client also receives 'cancelled' (and only that state) after its interrupt, with cancel_queued:true or without, synthesized from the `cancelled` list of the cloud session's own receipt (not the response that the host gets): for a uuid the host sent and did not cancel itself it means the cloud session dropped that command — it will not run; do not resend it; the frames follow the interrupt's success response, are not ordered against the interrupted turn's result, and unknown uuids (another client's prompt) may appear. From internal QueryEvent 'command_lifecycle'.

@internal Files a person attached to the conversation, each with the name the client showed its model for it, the most wanted first; at most 16. file_uuid is that of a file_attachments entry on a user message sent to this worker before the request. Only a worker that advertises file_names: true in turn_handoff_available uses the member, only on a request that names calls to run, and only when those calls run in the session's home directory: before they run, it copies each listed file it has downloaded into that directory, under that name, until a limit on time or on total size is reached, taking first the names that occur in the calls' own input. It replaces nothing then, skips a name it refuses or that the list holds twice, and, within one request, skips the further names of a file once it has found or placed one of them. If a person later sends another file under a name it placed, it puts that file's bytes in the copy's place, or removes the copy if it cannot, and only while the copy is still the file it placed, unchanged. The member is never a reason to refuse the request: a malformed one (a longer list included) is ignored whole, and the calls run whatever became of the copies.
@internal Fingerprint binding the harness section counts to the exact content they were computed against; a hook rewrite invalidates the counts rather than misplacing rewritten bytes

@internal Fire-and-forget push when a plugin's `$.ui.focus` (through the `ui.focus` chain) moved the focus ring of a site a remote surface draws onto one of its Buttons, Inputs or Selects: the surface focuses that element if it still draws it. The person's own moves (ui_focus requests) are never pushed back.

@internal Fire-and-forget push when a plugin's `$.ui.scroll` (through the `ui.scroll` chain) moved the window of a site a remote surface draws: the surface scrolls the site's body there. The person's own scrolls (ui_scroll requests) are never pushed back.

@internal For the program that starts Claude Code: read only from --settings at the launch; ignored in settings sent to a running session and in user, project, local and managed settings. Refuse reads outside the working directories, other than a shell command's, in every permission mode: reads by the file tools (Read, Grep, Glob, LSP) and by other built-in tools that send or publish a file, attachments, connectors' file inputs, Chrome uploads, memory recall, a project's CLAUDE.md includes and memory. No allow rule lifts it, and blockReadsExemptPaths applies to it. With it on, only the starting directory, --add-dir and the additionalDirectories of --settings or of settings sent later by that program (a full path, on Windows with its drive, or ~ or ~/…; a relative entry does not count) count as working directories, for it and for blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: the user, project, local and managed settings and /add-dir add none. Claude Code's own files stay readable: this project's and this session's files in its configuration folder, this project's memory unless a user, project or local settings file, or managed settings, chose that folder, and the CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, plugins, agents and commands in its configuration folder. It is blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories without that setting's hold on the shell: it does not limit shell commands, sandboxed or not, nor what MCP servers and the programs that hooks run read by themselves. Like that setting, it does not stop Claude Code loading skills, commands, agents, output styles and workflows from .claude folders above the working directory (as far as the repository's root; outside a repository, the home folder or the disk's root), nor through links in a .claude folder, the working directory's own included. It does not limit writes, but Edit and Write need an existing file read first, and where Read is refused only a shell command (such as cat) can do that. Cloud sessions (Claude Code on the web), whose file tools run in a container that is itself the boundary, may not apply it.
@internal Forwarded entries installed as callbacks.

@internal Fresh provider bearer token returned by the SDK host getHostAuthToken callback, or null if the credential was refreshed out-of-band. materialUnchanged is only consulted when authToken is null (out-of-band delivery) — true tells the CLI to fast-fail instead of backing off. A local AWS / Google Cloud credential-chain failure in the CLI is capped at two retries whatever the reply.

@internal Garbage collections on the CLI process's main thread, counted from early start-up, before its main modules load. to_first_message: up to the start of the process's first turn, whether a message or start-up itself (a resumed turn, say) began it; absent if no turn began first or its count failed. to_first_result: up to this result, including to_first_message's. A worker claimed from a warm spare counts from the spare's own start, so both include its wait for the claim. Each gives eden (collections of young objects only; under Bun the process's first also marks the whole heap), full (collections of the whole heap), wall_ms (their summed wall-clock time, not CPU time) and heap_after_mib (heap in use after the last one; absent if none ran). A collection still running at either moment is not in that count. Only on the process's first numbered result (result_index 0) within an hour of its start, only when the process, or the warm spare it was claimed from, started with CLAUDE_CODE_COUNT_GARBAGE_COLLECTIONS=1, and only from cloud workers that Anthropic hosts, with telemetry on, never from a session in claude-code-server.
@internal Hint to expand a side panel. Enum is a superset of AppState.expandedView for back-compat; do not narrow.
@internal Hook event name, as for inventory entries.
@internal Hook event name. A plain string rather than the HookEvent enum so an older worker tolerates an event it does not know: it ignores that entry instead of rejecting the whole registration.
@internal Hook kind on the device. prompt, agent and mcp_tool hooks are never forwarded; a new kind is a deliberate schema change.

@internal Host attestation that the user explicitly accepted a trust dialog for the session's working directory before launching it — the launch-time twin of set_cwd's trust_accepted/trusted_directory, for hosts whose dialog runs before the CLI is spawned and possibly on another machine than the ~/.claude.json this process reads (Claude Desktop's Code tab over SSH or WSL). Honored once, on the session's first initialize from the process that owns the CLI's stdin: the CLI records the working directory as trusted in the same store the interactive trust dialog writes (the home directory is trusted for the session only and never persisted), so the persisted-trust gates read the same answer they do in a checkout the user trusted at a terminal — project permission rules and hooks re-derive in the running process, the open-change announcement that follows this initialize already sees it, and readers evaluated at launch (project .mcp.json approval, project plugins, agent-frontmatter hooks and MCP servers) see it from the next launch on. A re-sent initialize, one arriving over a remote session transport, or one sent to a parked spare (--await-claim; send workspace_trust with claim_session instead) records nothing. workspace_trust_recorded in the response reports the outcome.

@internal How far along a task is, sent only to a mobile client that names `Progress` in `ui_attach`'s `draws`; for any other client the engine draws it as Box and Text. `label` names it, `value` is the fraction from 0 to 1 and absent while the task is running, `valueText` is the figure as a person reads it, `color` a theme key or a raw color. No children.

@internal How far the counter of a CPU accounting group moved in the process_cpu_ms_turn stretch: CPU time (user plus system) of the programs in that group. The shells of the Bash and Monitor tools join the group just before each command runs, so it holds those shells, everything they start, and any program that an earlier command, or an earlier Claude Code process that used the same group, left running there. It is not part of process_cpu_ms_turn, which leaves out child processes. A shell's own start-up is not counted. Nor is a command whose shell could not join the group, as can happen under Claude Code's command sandbox or CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX: the figure then reads lower, or 0, rather than being absent. Programs the CLI starts itself, such as hooks, MCP and LSP servers and plugin monitors, and a ! command that a person sends from the client, do not join the group. A command that the session sends to another machine, such as a linked computer, is in no field. Present where process_cpu_ms_turn is, if the CLI could make the group when its process started and could read its counter at the start and the end of the stretch, the second reading not lower than the first. The CLI makes the group only on Linux, where its process has a CPU accounting group of its own on a cgroup v1 hierarchy that carries cpuacct alone. Absent, never 0, otherwise.

@internal How long the thinking block in this frame took to stream, in whole milliseconds (at least 1): from its content_block_start to its content_block_stop, or to the interrupt that cut it, so the wait for the response's first token is not counted. For display only. Sent only on a frame whose one content block is a thinking block that was streamed. Older CLI versions never send it, and a CLI that rebuilt its history from SDK frames does not send it when it replays that history, so be ready to show the block without a duration. Wrapper-level sibling — never inside `message.content` — so it is not replayed to the model.

@internal How many times a safety system has stopped one of this session's model calls made through the query pipeline (main loop, subagents, forked skills, compaction and other internal calls), as a running total since the session started in this process; two sessions in one process keep separate counts. Counted: a response that ends on stop_reason refusal, whether Claude Code then shows it, retries it or re-sends it to another model; a refusal that the API itself answered on a fallback model; output that the API's content filter stopped for good (the stop ends the call); and, where the build can recognise it (public builds cannot), a server-side safety monitor's block (api_error safety_monitor_blocked). It counts these events, not calls: one call can add a refusal answered on a fallback model and then that model's own refusal. 0 means that none of these was seen; a kind of stop that this version does not know is not counted. Never sum across results. It is never saved, so a resumed session starts at 0 again, and a mid-session /clear zeroes it: over a stored log that spans a restart, a resume or a /clear, any result above 0 means a stop happened, and a later 0 does not cancel it. Present, 0 included, on every result that carries a turn's measured totals. Absent on the zeroed results that stand in for a crashed, cut or never-started turn, on Remote Control's results and from older producers, where it says nothing: absent is not 0. A call still running when a result is written (a background subagent's) shows on the next result; a result held back while background subagents finished carries the count as of when it is written to the stream, never less than it was built with. Not counted inside the pipeline: a stop of the API's content filter that Claude Code answers by streaming the request again (so 0 does not rule one out), an organization's data-loss-prevention denial (api_error dlp_request_denied), a block by a cloud provider's own guardrail, an advisor's refusal inside a reply that ends normally. Not counted at all: model calls outside the query pipeline (e.g. the permission classifier, token-count probes) and work in other processes.

@internal How many uploads carrying new visible reply text (as first_text_post_ms defines it) the remote transport sent during the turn, counting from the upload that first_text_post_ms measures until this result was built. Uploads still queued at that point are not counted, and a retry counts only if it carries text that no earlier upload did. Present only when first_text_post_ms is, and never in a claude-code-server tenant.

@internal How the request_build phase of time_to_request_phases_ms was spent: assembling the request from the normalized messages up to its dispatch. Read it as tool_schema_build_detail: the nine values from records_ms to other_ms, in the order the code runs, add up to the phase exactly. The phase pauses while the first attempt's client is made (client_creation), and that pause is in no part. records_ms: from the phase's start to the check for fallback blocks: recording for the conversation what this request sends (copies of tool inputs, tools surfaced or deferred) and setting up what the retry handlers share. system_ms: that check, a short hash of the first user message and the attribution header that carries it, the cache lifetime and the system prompt's blocks. headers_ms: comparing the tools and the system prompt with what was first sent and, where they changed and the model is told, passing that notice on and building the messages a second time with it; then effort, fast mode, up to two waits for the permission context, the beta headers that stay on for the conversation, and setting up the handling of the API's context hints, whose code can load here on a process's first request. cache_break_record_ms: recording the prompt's state (recordPromptState) so that a later prompt-cache break can be explained: a digest of every message and hashes of the system prompt and the tool list; where the session keeps that state on disk, a process's first request also reads the file and every request queues its write (in a cloud runner's session it is queued after the response instead, outside this phase, unless the model is one that cache-break detection skips). plans_ms: from there to the end of the request builder's definition, such as defining the first retry handlers, planning which tool results to clear and opening the request's tracing span. retry_setup_ms: from there to the making of the first attempt's client, such as defining the rest of the retry and fallback handlers. sent_build_ms: building the parameters that are sent, for every attempt before the first dispatch (normally one). record_attempt_ms: from there to the moment the request is recorded as sent: reading the values for the analytics event that logs the request (the event itself is sent after the dispatch and is timed nowhere), the debug log's detail, and the attempt's record, such as the check of the sent prefix and the request's capture. other_ms: as in tool_schema_build_detail. Three more members each measure one stretch inside the sent build; they lie within sent_build_ms, need not add up to it, and are not part of the sum. sent_build_safety_context_ms: assembling the context for the server-side safety check; near 0 where the session does not ask the server to check tool calls. sent_build_cache_breakpoints_ms: the last clean-up of the messages before sending, placing the prompt-cache breakpoints, which makes a new copy of every message, and the scans for cache markers that follow. sent_build_surrogate_scan_ms: reading every string of the body for lone UTF-16 surrogates, and the scrub where one is found. Nothing after the turn's first dispatch is timed (a retry, a later request), and nothing of a subagent's request or a side query. Present where time_to_request_phases_ms has request_build.

@internal How the time from frame_enqueued_wall_ms to turn_started_wall_ms was spent, in integer ms per step of the host's work through its message queue. Each step is where the host was at the time, which for part of the stretch may be an earlier message's turn. The steps: idle (the host was not working through its queue), earlier_turn (an earlier turn still running, including its work after its result), after_turn (the host's work after an earlier turn ended and before it took the next message: recording the outcome, writing the transcript and acknowledgements, and releasing the queue; also its handling of a crash), background_wait (waiting on background tasks before looking at the queue again), entry_joins (other waits when the host starts on its queue, before it may take a message), sdk_mcp_update (the claude -p host updating its SDK MCP servers when it starts on its queue), loop_top (reloading plugins that changed, at the start of each pass over the queue), session_start_wait (waiting for the plugins' first session.start hook, and taking the message off the queue), first_command (the claude -p host's waits for its plugin registry and a Projects mount before the first message it takes each time it starts on its queue), mcp_prewait (waiting for MCP servers still connecting, before that same first message), repo_wait (a claude-code-server session waiting for its repository before a turn), turn_joins (before every turn: waiting for a Projects mount and for SDK or newly added MCP servers), tool_pool (building the turn's tools), commit (marking the message taken and setting up its turn), after_arm (waiting for a cleared permission prompt's record to be written, and the host's other work once the turn is set up), turn_gate (work the host requires before every turn), turn_open (the host's turn-start hook and other turn setup), engine_setup (getting the engine for the turn; on the claude -p host's first turn, building its session), tool_reread (re-reading tools, MCP clients and settings for the turn), cwd (switching to the turn's working directory), and other (the rest: rounding, and the wall clock running ahead of the monotonic one). Values are rounded so that they add up: each is within 1 ms of its step's time, a step that comes out as 0 is absent, and other is always present. The values sum to turn_started_wall_ms minus frame_enqueued_wall_ms, except that they can exceed it, usually by 1 ms from rounding and by more if the wall clock stepped back. Present only when frame_received_wall_ms is, and absent from older producers.

@internal How the tool_schema_build phase of time_to_request_phases_ms was spent, in whole ms, in the order the code runs, over the main-conversation requests built before the turn's first dispatch (normally one). The six _ms values add up to that phase exactly. Each is rounded so that a fraction of a ms carries into the next, so each can read up to 1 ms more or less than its own time. betas_ms: choosing the beta headers, reading what the model supports and the thinking configuration. waits_ms: waiting for the account's Artifact capabilities, which the Artifact tool's schema lists; building early the schema of each tool that a plugin's tool.describe hook may move in or out of the tool list; and deciding whether tool search is on, which can measure the MCP tools' descriptions; on a later turn each usually returns at once. placement_ms: deciding which tools the request declares in full, which deferred and which by reference, with the waits that takes, such as the permission context and, on the conversation's first request in the process, the recorded tools of MCP servers still connecting. render_ms: making the API schema of every declared tool; a tool whose schema is cached, or that is sent as the conversation recorded it, skips the build. after_ms: the rest of the phase, such as building the schemas of tools the conversation defines inside its messages, kept for a retry that must list them with the other tools instead, and applying the plan for deferred tools. other_ms: time that no part covers plus what rounding leaves: 0 or 1 unless some stretch of the phase has no mark. Where an error stopped a build part-way and the request was built again before the first dispatch, the phase leaves out the unfinished stretch but the parts keep it, so the last parts are cut to fit. tools is how many tools the render made schemas for. new_schemas is how much the tool-schema cache grew over the phase (one cache per process, shared with the session's subagents and side queries; on claude-code-server one per tenant). That is about how many schemas were built from scratch in any part of the phase: 0 on most later turns, near tools on a process's first turn, and near 0 where the tools are sent as a resumed conversation recorded them. Entries the cache dropped meanwhile are taken off, and entries that another request added meanwhile are counted. Where the request was built more than once before the dispatch, tools and new_schemas are the last build's. Present where time_to_request_phases_ms has tool_schema_build.

@internal How the triggering send's frame spent the time from frame_received_wall_ms to frame_enqueued_wall_ms, in integer ms per step: before_read (until the input loop read the frame; a frame received more than once counts from the earliest receipt no earlier copy already took), and, carved out of before_read where the loop could tell them apart, startup_wait (the part before the input loop existed, the worker still starting), control_requests_ahead (the part the loop spent handling control requests before it read the frame) and user_frames_ahead (the part it spent on earlier user frames, each from its read until the loop moved on, at its delivery or its parking), so that before_read keeps only the rest (frames handled without being noted, and everything when no split could be made); then dedup, flag_settle, receive_hook, attachments, admission_wait (held behind a pending model switch, a pending MCP server-set change, start-up work the worker still owed its first turn, or an earlier held frame), admit_check (the host's decision whether to queue the frame, when it had to be awaited), and other (the rest). Steps that did not run are absent; before_read and other are always present. The values sum to frame_enqueued_wall_ms minus frame_received_wall_ms, unless other or before_read came out negative and was set to 0. Present exactly when frame_received_wall_ms is, except from older producers.

@internal How time_to_request_ms was spent, in integer ms per phase, summing to it exactly: system_prompt, resume_other (settling, before the turn's own prompt, tool calls that an earlier run left open or the session's client handed over, see turn_start_resume_kind; excluding four parts of it that have keys of their own: resume_store_confirm, writing a handed-over turn's lines to the transcript and waiting for the store to confirm them; resume_staged_files_wait, that turn's wait for files its client is still staging; resume_connector_wait, an orphaned permission's wait for its tool's MCP server to connect; turn_start_tool_run, the calls' permission checks, a person's time at a prompt included, and their runs, which are work the user asked for, not preparation; older producers report these five as one key, turn_start_resume), process_user_input (excluding four parts of it that have keys of their own: input_images, input_attachments, input_command, input_hooks), conversation_append (from the end of process_user_input to the start of tool_pool_refresh, less transcript_persist: running the host's callback that comes before the turn's input, which can add messages of its own; labelling the turn's messages and adding them to the conversation, first waiting for any messages the host is still adding, and through any hooks that see messages as they are added; carrying over a typed /compact's task list; on a claude-code-server tenant, sending an early request for the IP address of the person who sent the message, waiting until it has left but not for the answer; starting the transcript write; and building the copies of the turn's messages that are echoed back to the client), transcript_persist, tool_pool_refresh, system_prompt_rebuild (a second assembly of the system prompt, run when the tool pool re-read after the message was handled differs from the turn-start pool; older producers report it inside system_prompt), init_message, init_frame_send (from the end of init_message to the start of engine_pickup: sending the system/init frame and the host's handling of it, where the host can start generating the session's title; then sending hook notices and a local command's output, the once-per-session checks of the instruction files' size (CLAUDE.md and the like) and of missing settings, and raising the turn.start event for plugins; a turn that sends its init before resume_other, which is a handed-over turn or, after a worker restart, a re-run of calls that run on another machine, counts that frame's sending here too and times the rest from where an ordinary turn would send its init), engine_pickup, loop_entry (from the end of engine_pickup to the start of message_prep, less memory_recall_wait and memory_context_wait: a wait of at most 1.5 s for the list of Artifact tool actions the account may use, when the turn offers that tool and no list is saved for the account; deciding whether the session's context, such as instruction files, is written into the start of the request or sent as messages of its own; starting the memory fetches; delivering events and messages queued for the turn's start; and the host's handling of each message these steps and the memory waits add), memory_recall_wait, memory_context_wait, message_prep, model_config_wait, autocompact, request_announcements (from the end of autocompact to the start of query_setup, less the model choice made in this stretch, whose wait is counted in model_config_wait: right after a compaction, the context announced again and the compaction's own messages; any work queued to run between the model's tool calls; PostModelSwitch hook output; git status and project docs read for the announcements, the docs only after any PreToolUse hooks have allowed the read; the notices and announcements put ahead of the request, about usage limits, the session's files, credentials, commit and PR attribution, the advisor tool and the context itself; the system prompt's copy recorded in the transcript; and the host's handling of each message these add and of the rows for events delivered at the turn's start), query_setup, auto_mode_context_wait (the wait at dispatch for the auto-mode context, on a request that started one), model_gates, tool_schema_build, message_normalization, client_creation, request_build, then at most one of redrive_reactive_compact, redrive_fallback_model, redrive_non_streaming and redrive_other (present when the first model request of the turn never began streaming, or was answered without streaming, so time_to_request_ms runs to the send time of a later request: the time between the two sends, named for the reason; after a reply without streaming it includes that reply and any tool calls), and other (the remainder no phase covers). A phase that did not run on the turn is absent; other is always present. Producers that predate conversation_append, init_frame_send, loop_entry and request_announcements count that time in other. Present where time_to_request_ms is, on CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE sessions and hosts that set CLAUDE_CODE_EMIT_STARTUP_TIMING; absent elsewhere and from older producers.

@internal How to find the file `path` names, instead of resolving it against the live cwd, which a `cd` in the shell moves. workspace_root, diff_root and repo each name a directory the session looks up on each request; as_written names none, and has its contract in its own description. workspace_root is the root list_directory lists from. diff_root is the repository get_workspace_diff diffs, so a path taken from that diff opens the file the diff shows. It is refused in a session whose diff follows the shell's cwd between several repositories; a client that knows the repository should send `repo`. repo is the checkout the session declares for that repository or, failing that, diff_root when its origin remote ends in that owner/name. With those three, `path` must stay inside that directory as spelled (the check follows no symlink). Whatever the anchor, the read is gated as any other read_file is. A path that is `~`, starts with `~/` or leaves that directory, or an anchor the session cannot resolve or does not serve, is refused with the error `read denied: <path>`. Leave the field out when there is no anchor: null is refused. A CLI that predates this field ignores it and reads against the live cwd; the response's `anchor` tells the two apart.
@internal ISO 8601 UTC instant the lease expires (no offset), as Date.prototype.toISOString renders it.
@internal Ids of the ignored entries.

@internal In how many chunks the runtime's fetch handed over the bodies of those streams. It is not the number of socket reads, several of which can make one chunk. Against main_stream_event_count it shows how the API's events arrive grouped, though the two do not divide evenly: a chunk can end inside an event, keepalive comments and pings are chunks that bring no event, and a stream that failed or was aborted can count one chunk whose events were never read. Absent, never 0, when a stream's chunks were not counted, as on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle, with the byte watchdog off, or for a stream still open when this result is built.

@internal Input only. Asks the CLI to put this prompt back in its queue, instead of losing it, when an interrupt crosses with a running turn taking the prompt in: the interrupt was sent while its sender still believed the prompt was waiting. The value says for how long an interrupt is taken to have been sent so: a whole number of milliseconds from 1, and above 10000 it counts as 10000. The time runs from the moment the turn announces the model request that carries the prompt (system/status 'requesting', which is on the wire only with partial messages); until then it has not begun. The prompt is put back when an interrupt control request without cancel_queued stops that turn within the time and before the model's next reply has begun to arrive. It goes back to the front of the queue under the same uuid and runs in a later turn of its own, after any queued prompt of higher priority; prompts queued behind it are not merged into that turn's prompt, though the turn can take them in as any turn does. The interrupt's response lists it under still_queued and under put_back, and from then on cancel_async_message can withdraw it. The stopped turn reports no 'cancelled' for it, counts it in its result's queued_turn_count (if its origin is stamped user-driven, as for any queued prompt) and leaves it out of that result's user_message_uuids (on an error result an empty list, with no user_message_uuid, if nothing else is listed). On stdout it reports command_lifecycle 'queued' a second time; over a remote transport its delivery is not reported 'processed' until its later turn ends. With cancel_queued:true it stays with the stopped turn and is not listed under the response's cancelled. The row the stopped turn wrote for it (a queued_command attachment) leaves the conversation and is never stored, so the model sees the prompt once; until the prompt can no longer be put back, that row and the rows after it are kept out of the stored transcript. UserPromptSubmit hooks run for it twice, and what they added to the stopped turn stays. If a compaction begins while that row is kept out, the row is stored at once and stays in the conversation, so the prompt, if an interrupt puts it back or has just done so, is seen twice. A prompt is put back at most once, and never after the host's own cancel_async_message for it answered cancelled:false. Of several prompts taken in since the model last spoke, only the last can be put back; the others stay with the stopped turn. The field is ignored when it is not such a number, when the message has no uuid or has shouldQuery:false, and when the message is not a person's own typing: a synthetic, hidden, client-composed, seeded, peer or relayed message, one that declares a non-human origin, or one whose client_platform names no app or keyboard that a person types in. claude-code-server also needs a client_platform, and one that names an app. A CLI that does not advertise interrupt_requeue_taken_v1 on system/init ignores the field too.

@internal Layout props on Box (`key` makes it a hover scope; `position` "absolute" with integer `top`/`left`/`right`/`bottom` cell offsets places it over its surroundings, out of the flow), color and style props on Text (with `size`, `weight`, `mono` and `tabular`, which each surface draws its own way; `bold` is true for a `semibold` or `bold` weight, and a `bold: true` with no weight also carries `weight: "semibold"`), spacing on Box in cells (on `desktop` and `mobile` also a step name, `xs` to `xl`), a `style` declaration string on div/span/b; the allowlisted subset the engine validated before the tree crossed.

@internal Lowercase hex SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes of a text doc's whole text; never on a project_read that delivered only part of the doc. Set where docVersionsOffered; also, while tengu_lovely_rain is on, on a project_read that saved the whole text to a file, and on a project_write by local_path in a conversation (not a script's inner call). A later checked write by path looks for this hash.
@internal Lowercase hex sha256 of the decoded content; must be one of the worker's own table digests for this template.
@internal MCP protocol metadata passed through to SDK consumers, never sent to the model (from internal UserMessage.mcpMeta).

@internal MCP server config entries from --mcp-config that failed validation and were skipped (e.g. a `url` entry with no `type`). Affected servers are absent from `mcp_servers[]`. `type` is a stable category from an open set — currently unknown_type, url_missing_type, invalid_config, reserved_name, or (Remote Control child only) bridge_carrier_foreign_entry, bridge_carrier_not_http, bridge_carrier_url_mismatch, bridge_carrier_no_ingress_origin, bridge_carrier_no_session_id; treat values you do not recognize as a generic skip. The key is omitted when there are no errors; CI can fail on `(mcp_server_errors?.length ?? 0) > 0`. On connections that persist frames server-side (the local bridge-worker lane) this key is always omitted — the skipped-entry detail stays in the local log, so an omitted key there does NOT assert every entry validated.

@internal MCP tools that run code the model writes, keyed by server name as registered, each with its tool names. In auto mode no allow rule, skill, hook or plugin approves a call to one on its own: the classifier judges it, unless set_mcp_permission_mode_override pins its server to default. Declaring any also stops every PermissionRequest hook allow from changing the permission mode (its setMode update is dropped). Give names without the mcp__ prefix: a server or tool name that starts with mcp__ is skipped as malformed. Read from the first initialize only; its response lists what was declared in code_running_mcp_tools_applied. See Options.codeRunningMcpTools.

@internal Major page faults (waits for memory to be read from disk) by the process in the time_to_request_cpu_ms window; Windows also counts faults needing no disk read. On a virtual machine, memory the host restores is not counted: the machine never sees those faults. Present where time_to_request_cpu_ms is.
@internal Minted once per device client process and stable across its reconnects and re-registrations; the owner key in the worker's store and the first segment of every hook id.

@internal Moves the session to a new working directory — the headless twin of /cd, for SDK hosts like Claude Desktop. Runs the same validation, Cd(...) permission rules, and relocation path as the interactive command, with the trust prompt delegated to the host via the needs_trust response arm. Before the first turn the move re-anchors start-of-session state (the first request is built as for a start in the new directory, no move notice); after a turn the prefix is preserved and the move arrives as an appended notice. SessionStart hooks are never re-run by set_cwd (those of the launch directory already ran and their output stays in the session); a host that starts the process before its directory is known should use --await-claim and claim_session, which run them in the bound directory instead. Rejected while a turn is in flight, and, on a Remote Control session, when it comes from a remote client rather than from the process that owns the CLI's stdin.

@internal No person typed this message's text in this session (a server or an app composed it). The text is delivered as written and is not treated as typing: no slash-command dispatch, no at-mention expansion beyond the message's own uploaded files, no reminder or command from keywords in it, and a skill named in it does not count as typed by the user. Who sent the message, and whether a person is present, stays with its origin. A Workflow does not relay the text to its agents as the user's request, unless a server-verified relay delivered it. Auto mode's local classifier and investigator do not read this mark: they go by the origin. Unlike client_composed, the turn-start attachment pass still runs. Any value other than false or null is read as true.

@internal Of the time from frame_enqueued_wall_ms to turn_started_wall_ms, the integer ms in which the claude -p host's message reader was held by control requests (such as mcp_set_servers or set_permission_mode) instead of reading the next message; for a request handled in the background, only its start counts. The host can keep working toward the turn meanwhile, so this overlaps turn_start_phases_ms and is not part of its sum. Absent when 0. A claude-code-server tenant's results never have this field.

@internal On a hand-back: the note the harness composed above the frame line in `body`, without the indent. On a blocked report it quotes the review's reason, which can quote the report, so show it as untrusted text. Absent when there is no note.

@internal On a hand-back: the subagent's report as the model reads it, under the frame line in `body`, without the indent. Draw it as a separate element from `handbackNote`: the two fields are their only boundary. Absent wherever `body` is and on a message that is not a hand-back.

@internal On a prompt that joins several queued messages from this sender: the joined messages in the order the model reads them, each with its own `body`. The origin's `body` is then absent. Absent on a message that was not joined and when any joined message had no `body`.

@internal On a turn that the session's client handed over (turn_start_resume_kind is turn_handoff), how long its turn_handoff control request waited from its arrival on the session server's SSE stream (--sdk-url) until the input loop read it, in integer ms on the monotonic clock, split into parts that frame_intake_phases_ms explains: startup_wait, control_requests_ahead and user_frames_ahead, each absent when 0, and before_read (the rest), always present. The values sum to the wait. Present only on results that carry turn_start_resume_kind. Absent on a claude-code-server tenant, when the host had handled too much since the arrival to say what the request waited behind, and from older producers.

@internal On the local-command twin, the run that printed the row: the command's name as `command.run` carried it (no slash), its arguments as the echo shows them (`***` when the command marks them sensitive) and, for a command a plugin registered, that plugin's name, or, for a row whose text plugins' `command.run` hooks answered or retold, the names the text is led by (untrusted text; absent for the binary's own command in its own words). Present when a `local` command's dispatch printed the row or a `command.run` hook answered it, absent on a never-ran notice. A surface that draws the hooks engine's `CommandOutput` site asks ui_render with these, the twin's text and its uuid as instance_id; toInternalMessages round-trips it onto the rebuilt row. Wrapper-level sibling — never inside `message.content`.

@internal On the local-command twin, what the row reports, so a host can offer a fix instead of relaying the text: 'unavailable_headless' (an interactive-panel command this session cannot open), 'unknown' (no command has the typed name), 'failed' (the command ran and failed), 'restart_required' (the change applies after Claude Code restarts). Absent when the row reports none of these; new kinds are additive, so treat an unknown one as absent. toInternalMessages round-trips it onto the rebuilt row. Wrapper-level sibling — never inside `message.content`.
@internal One forwarded device hook: identity and routing data only — never a command line, URL, path, header or condition text.
@internal One painted run over the text a ui_prompt_fill carries, normalized by the engine: clamped to the text, grapheme-aligned, never empty.
@internal One row per requested template.

@internal One to eight uuids (case ignored) of user messages whose turn this Stop is for; any other value is read as absent. The current turn is the latest one dequeued for a client's message (it may be over, or not yet started), with every turn started and message taken in since. A Stop that names one of its messages is handled as a plain interrupt (if latched, see still_queued, only for pending work that it names or that answers no client's message), and so is any Stop while the CLI knows of no current turn. Other Stops do nothing and get turn: 'spared', except a few that name work that is queued or, on claude -p, read and not yet queued (sparesCurrentTurn). Always include the message that opened the turn (user_message_uuid on its first frames, before any re-run): after a restart the CLI knows no other. A turn handed over by turn_handoff has no name: any Stop may stop it, so send a plain one. The uuids are only compared: never stored, logged, sent back or shown to the model. Not read beside cancel_queued:true or send_now:true, nor by older CLIs, which answer without turn.
@internal One-line summary shown to the user in the terminal when an asyncRewake hook exits with code 2. Defaults to "Stop hook feedback".

@internal Only on init frames written by the headless stream-json client of a cloud-hosted session (agent loop in the cloud container; this machine may be bound to it as a device): a snapshot per frame, absent in every other mode; no user, assistant or result frame precedes the first such init (informational system frames may; so may a worker's result that no init preceded, after all that was held ahead of it; on a re-attach so may frames of a turn already in progress, other clients' prompts, and the echo of this host's own prompt when the session already had it or it joins a turn in progress). `id` is the cloud session id, always in its `session_…` spelling (the producer normalizes the service's `cse_…` spelling of the same session); hosts store it and pass it back verbatim to re-attach. The frame-level `session_id` is instead the cloud worker's id, a uuidv5 of the session id in its `cse_` form: the same for the life of the cloud session across worker restarts and re-attaches until a /clear in the session, and passed through by the client unchanged. When `device.status` is `unbound`, `reason` is one of the client's unbound-reason keys and `message` its phrase: one line, at most 200 characters, no ANSI or trailing newline, worded to follow `Laptop tools unavailable: `. `directory_sync`: see docs/cloud-session-block.md. `not_applied`, when present, lists what the host passed that this session does not apply — `name` is a flag as `--flag`, a key inside --settings / --managed-settings as `settings.<key>` / `managed-settings.<key>`, or a field of the opening initialize as `initialize.<field>` (at most 40, lost first, each one line of about 64 characters at most); `kind` says what it costs: `lost` (the session does without something this invocation asked for — the informational warning names these), `kept` (an attach: the existing session keeps what it was created with) or `preference` (a display or host preference nobody would miss — the informational notice names these two), so a host may show them itself once or never; absent when nothing was left unapplied. `host`, when present, is what this machine announces as to the session: `handle` is the name the model addresses it by (and a client shows), `working_dir` the absolute directory served calls run in (that machine's separators), `platform` its platform word, `cli_version` its Claude Code version; each one line of at most 200 characters; present once this machine has built an announce for the session (bound, with something or an explicit nothing to serve), absent otherwise and on clients that predate it. `serving`, when present, says whether this machine serves its tools (Bash, Read, Write, Edit) to the session over the session's channel: `state` is `pending` while bound and about to announce, `on` once the session holds this machine's tools, `off` when it serves nothing, `revoked` when it stopped mid-session; `reason` (present when `state` is not `on` and the cause is known) is one of the client's serving-off keys — `not_bound` (see `device.reason`), `external_build`, `windows`, `muted` (Anthropic's emergency switch turned serving off; it comes back when the switch does), `switch_off`, `launched_from_home`, `channel_off`, `egress`, `policy_org` (the organization does not allow remote sessions), `flag_off`, `flag_stale`, `announce_refused`, `announce_unverified`, `computer_too_old` (Claude Code on this machine is too old for the session), `session_too_old` (the session's Claude Code is too old for this machine), `superseded` — an open set: render an unrecognized value as a generic not-serving state; `policy` is the serving policy in effect (`parity`, or the stricter `interim` fallback); `channel` is `session`, or `bridge_only` when the session channel is switched off on this machine and served calls (if any) ride only the legacy device bridge, whose state this block does not describe. Absent on clients that predate it: feature-detect the key. `connection`, when present, is this client's stream to the session: `connecting` before it first connects, `live` while it is up, `reconnecting` while it is lost and being re-dialled (this machine is offline to the session meanwhile). `calls`, when present (once this machine has served a call this attach), is what it serves right now and how its last calls ended, by id and tool name only — never a call's input or output: `live` lists, oldest first, each call admitted here and not yet ended, `state` `running` while this machine executes it or `asked` while it waits on the session's approval (`ask_id` names the question; `since` is when it entered that state and `lapses_at` about when the session gives an unanswered question up, both epoch milliseconds on this machine's clock — the session's own timer decides); `recent` lists, newest last, at most 20 calls that ended here, `ended` being `completed`, `denied` (the session said no), `withdrawn` (the session took the question back unanswered — its patience ran out or the turn moved on), `refused` or `failed`, with `code` the result's disposition, refusal or failure word when it has one, and `at` when. `notices`, when present, is what this machine's serving has told the person during this attach that a host should show, at most 8: `key` is the notice's stable name (an open set — `device-mcp-consent`: this machine has MCP servers a cloud session could use and none are offered until the person allows it; `device-mcp-reconsent`: a server it offers changed the tools it lists and is withheld until re-approved, or this machine's record of what its servers list could not be read and none are offered — `text` says which; `device-mcp-policy`: a deny list in this machine's Claude Code settings lists remote-devices, so none of its MCP servers are offered; `device-mcp-dropped`; `served-hooks-not-run`; `served-hook-errors`; `served-bash-launched-from-home`; `served-tools-muted` / `served-tools-unmuted`; `announce_unverified`; `computer_too_old` / `session_too_old`) and `text` its one line (at most 200 characters, no ANSI or newline) — this machine's own words with names from its own configuration, to be shown as plain text; written only by a serve-only helper (`--attach-serve`) and absent when nothing was said. `calls`, `connection` and `notices` are pushed between inits on `cloud_session_delta` frames. `client_version` rises only on a breaking change to this block — warn and continue on a higher value, never refuse; `not_applied[].kind`, `serving.state`, `connection`, `calls[].state` / `ended` and reason keys may gain values without it changing, so treat unrecognized values neutrally (an unrecognized `serving.state` as not serving — this schema itself parses an unrecognized `serving.state` as `off`, `policy` as `interim`, `channel` as `bridge_only`).

@internal Only on the URL prompt that WebFetch raises mid-call, when the session's web-fetch proxy refuses an address. Says whether the session's line of such prompts was on for this call. 'one_at_a_time' = on: the call took a turn in the line, so no other prompt of that line was up when this one was raised. 'all_at_once' = off: the call joined no line, and its prompt was raised without waiting. For the host's logs: nothing in the CLI decides by it, and a host should not either.

@internal Only true, and only with an empty tool_use_ids: the user stopped this turn while its last message, an assistant message holding calls that have not run, was being handed over. The worker appends the turn, closes those calls and marks the turn exactly as when a turn of its own is stopped before a call runs, and ends it with the result a stopped turn ends with; when an earlier delivery already appended the turn, the calls are closed in place.
@internal Opt-in break reminder. When enabled, shows a dismissible nudge after sustained continuous use. Never blocks — just a friendly heads-up.
@internal Opt-in quiet hours. When enabled, shows a single soft nudge per session while inside the configured local-time window. Never blocks.

@internal Output only, and to be read only on a message the CLI wrote, never on one another client of the session posted: on a session event, only where its `source` is `worker`. On a message a plugin sent, what a host can show under the plugin's name in place of `message`. `name` is that name as the wrapper the model reads prints it, on one line and scrubbed; `origin.name` holds it raw. `text` is the prompt as hooks left it, with prompts merged into one turn joined by newlines, when `message` is exactly the wrapper the model reads around that prompt. Or it is the command the plugin ran as a person would type it, such as `/review 12`, when `message` is only that command's tags and `text` holds all their words; arguments can make it more than one line, so show all of it. Absent on any other message, and on a prompt sent as the person's own words; there, show `message`.

@internal Parameters of api_error, present only for the kinds that have any. effort: the effort level the API refused (effort_requires_thinking). media (media_removed): the kind of block the API refused; absent for media_budget. media_reason (media_removed): unsupported_by_model — the API said that the model does not accept PDF documents; media_budget — the request's images and documents together exceed the API's limit, and the requests that follow may leave out blocks of either kind; unprocessable — every other refusal, a gateway's report of a model's refusal among them. provider: the API provider whose credentials failed (provider_credentials, gateway_session_expired). remedy (provider_credentials, gateway_session_expired): refresh_command — a configured refresh command (awsAuthRefresh / gcpAuthRefresh) refreshes the credentials; refresh_credentials — refresh the provider's credentials by hand, no command is configured; adc — refresh the Google application default credentials or the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS key file; gateway_token — replace the gateway token supplied through ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN or ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS; host_managed — the host application owns these credentials; model_access — the credentials work but the model is not enabled for this account and region (Amazon Bedrock). rate_limit_info (usage_limit_reached): what the refused request's own response said about the limit, in the shape rate_limit_event carries. It is read from the same values as the message text, so its status, limit and reset are the text's: status is rejected and isUsingOverage false, rateLimitType names the limit, resetsAt is when it resets, and overageStatus, overageResetsAt, overageDisabledReason and limitScope say whose spend cap it is (the person's own cap arrives as org_level_disabled_until, as on rate_limit_event); dailyCapPaused is true when usage is paused for the organization; no other member is sent. It is that refusal's record and is never updated, so compare resetsAt with the clock before calling the limit current. rate_limit_info (model_requires_usage_credits): that refusal's record, read from the same headers as the message text: status is rejected and isUsingOverage false; rateLimitType is the response's claim (seven_day_overage_included when an included allowance was used up) and is absent when it named none; resetsAt, overageStatus, overageResetsAt and limitScope come when the response had them; errorCode is credits_required when the body said so; overageDisabledReason is the disabled-reason header's when that header came with a claim or overage status, else the body's (the message text can also fall back to a reason cached from an earlier response, which the record does not carry); canUserPurchaseCredits and hasChargeableSavedPaymentMethod come from the body; the person's own cap arrives as org_level_disabled_until, as on rate_limit_event; no other member is sent. cut (max_output_tokens): which stop reason of the API cut the reply short, which max_output_tokens alone does not say: output_limit — max_tokens, the request's output-token maximum; context_window — model_context_window_exceeded, the model's context window. Absent on the one other error that carries max_output_tokens, the API's tool_use_block_cut_off, which api_error_code names.

@internal Pauses (true) or un-pauses (false) the session's prompt suggestions at runtime, for a host whose composer is not on screen: while paused, no turn end starts a suggestion, and the first turn end after paused is set back to false does. The state is one boolean in this CLI process, on top of the initialize request's promptSuggestions option and the user's own setting, neither of which it changes: a respawned or resumed session starts unpaused, so the host must send it again, and with two clients attached one client's pause applies to both. Acknowledged with an empty success; a CLI build where this is not yet enabled acknowledges and keeps generating, and an older CLI answers an unknown-subtype error.

@internal Per-OS variant of policyHelper, keyed by platform: macos, linux, windows, wsl, plus an optional "default" entry that is a STATIC settings payload (a JSON object of managed settings, not a helper). Each per-OS entry carries a helper — a "path", or an inline "script" + "interpreter" delivered to a fixed interpreter over stdin, either with timeoutMs/refreshIntervalMs — its own static "defaultSettings" payload, or both; an entry may be payload-only. Selection for a platform walks its chain (the platform's own entry; on wsl the linux entry next): the first helper on the chain wins over policyHelper; if no helper is configured — or the selected helper fails at startup or refresh — the first payload applies (the chain's "defaultSettings" in platform-specific-first order, then the top-level "default", applied with no process spawned; unrecognized platforms reach only "default"); with no payload either, policyHelper. Honored from admin-controlled policy sources, and from remote managed settings — a payload of plain policy as delivered, like any other remote key; a helper, or a payload carrying anything the managed-settings approval dialog lists, only once the settings are verified this session and approved there (policyHelper itself is never honored from remote).

@internal Per-model usage and cost of the calls this process counted since it wrote its previous result (since it started, for its first), keyed and shaped like modelUsage and covering the same calls. Sum it over a conversation's results instead of subtracting modelUsage totals: within a conversation each call is stated on at most one result, whatever a resume or a kill does to modelUsage. Calls that finish after a result (a background subagent, a late title call) are stated on the next result, and a /clear's own result states what was counted before it. Nothing is carried from one process to the next, so what a process counted after its last result is stated nowhere. That includes the finished calls of a turn in flight when the process is shut down or killed, even where another process carries the turn on and writes its result. A result whose write fails loses its usage too (result_index shows the gap). A Workflow agent that runs as a cloud session of its own is counted here, as in modelUsage, and that session's own results state it too. costBasis, canonicalModel and provider are the latest request's. A model with nothing counted is left out; {} means nothing was counted. Set by a stream-json or --sdk-url run on the results it numbers as it writes them; a result relayed from another process keeps what that process set. Not set on error results numbered by hand (a start-up failure, an error that escapes the run), by --output-format json and text runs, or by older versions. Absent is not {}.

@internal Per-window usage for the session (5-hour), weekly (7-day), and overage-included weekly (per-model bucket; present only for accounts whose responses carry that window) subscription rate-limit windows, as read from the anthropic-ratelimit-unified-* response headers. utilization is the fraction of the window used (usually 0-1, same scale as the top-level utilization field; values above 1 occur when usage legitimately runs past a window's cap, e.g. lower-priority episodes past the 5-hour limit); resetsAt is unix epoch seconds. status is the status the server sent for the window: allowed_warning once past a warning threshold, rejected at or past its limit. A rejected window alone does not mean requests are refused; the top-level status says whether they are. surpassedThreshold is the highest warning threshold passed, as a fraction of the limit (1 once rejected). Each is absent when the server sent none or a value this version cannot read. Unlike the top-level status/utilization fields, which describe the currently limiting window, every window is tracked on every observation, and events are emitted when a window's rounded percentage, reset time, status or threshold moves, not only on status transitions. Windows absent from the account state are absent here. Absent until the first response carrying these headers is observed, and always absent for API-key, Bedrock, and Vertex sessions, whose responses do not carry them.

@internal Plugin authoring feedback (e.g., a default folder shadowed by a manifest key). When `plugin` matches an entry in `plugins[]`, that plugin loaded and the warning is advisory; warnings with a synthetic `plugin` source (no matching `plugins[]` entry, e.g. workspace-level suppression notices) describe content that did NOT load. The key is omitted when there are no warnings. On connections that persist frames server-side (the local bridge-worker lane) this key is always omitted — plugin diagnostics stay in the local log, so an omitted key there does NOT assert a clean load.
@internal Plumbing tools the machine answers over remote_plumbing_call for the session's own machinery; never model-facing.

@internal PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure hooks whose matcher can only match file-writing tools. The worker never forwards after-edit events for those tools (the device copy of the file is stale or absent), so such a hook could never fire and is not sent.

@internal Present ('mcp-task') only on a notification that an MCP server's own task has ended, and not on every one. Narrower than task_type 'mcp_task', which also covers an MCP tool call moved to the background.

@internal Present ('session-task') when the notification reports on work this session itself launched: a background agent, shell command, workflow, monitor, MCP or remote task settling, a detached tool call, or a hook rewake or worker check-in following up on such work. Absent on webhook, artifact and other externally-authored deliveries.

@internal Present on the line that ends a submitted prompt before a model call. It says how the prompt ended, so a host can write its own message or count endings and does not match `content`. kind: 'blocked_by_hook' (a hook answered with a block), 'stopped_by_hook' (a hook answered continue:false), 'dropped_by_hook' (a plugin's code module dropped the prompt), 'not_passed_on' (a plugin's code module answered and did not pass the prompt on), 'no_verdict' (no hook gave a verdict, and Claude Code ended the prompt itself). prompt_kept: true when the prompt stays in the conversation, where the model reads it on the next turn. Do not infer it from kind. reason: the hook's text as Claude Code got it, with nothing added here; a model writes it for a prompt or agent hook. It is never sent with no_verdict. It is absent when Claude Code got no text, and for a plugin's code module that blocks on the UserPromptSubmit hook event. ANSI codes are removed, control and invisible characters are replaced, line feeds stay, and long text is cut. It is untrusted and can quote the prompt, so render it as plain text. A cloud session can run the hook on another machine: its tool container, where any program can write reason, or the person's own machine. reason is then what that machine sent, for a block and for a stop. The person's own machine puts a label before the stderr of an exit 2, or before 'No stderr output' when there is none. Either machine makes the block itself when it could not read all of the hook's output, and the person's own machine can do so when its timeout fires. Each reads 'blocked_by_hook', with that machine's sentence as reason. Claude Code's own block for an SDK host that reconnected before its hook answered reads the same way, with Claude Code's sentence as reason. New values can appear: treat an unknown value as absent, and ignore reason beside an unknown kind. A slash command that runs as a fork does not send this key when a hook ends it. A follow-up that a hook blocks while a turn runs carries this key too, so read it as the end of a turn only when the next result has num_turns 0.

@internal Present on the warning that says a requested model was refused and the session uses another, so a host can word the notice itself instead of reading `content`. Both names are cleaned as they are in `content`: model-id characters only, cut to 128 with a trailing …, or '(unrecognized model name)' when none are left. They are still untrusted text: render them as plain text. requested_model: the refused model as it was asked for, or the id that a refused Default pick stood for. effective_model: the model in use when the line was built; a later switch can outdate it. at: 'start' for the model the process chose when it started (from --model, the environment, settings or --agent's frontmatter), 'switch' for anything later: a pick, an agent seated by initialize or when a pre-warmed process is claimed, a model kept at a turn's end. 'resume' is never on the wire: it marks a saved row alone, the notice that a resumed session's model could not be restored. An unknown value reads as absent.
@internal Present only when the feedback-survey surface is enabled for this host (GrowthBook gate, privacy level, and org policy all allow it). Absent means the host must not show the survey.

@internal Present when ANY hop of this banner's multi-hop episode was a cyber refusal — not only the origin hop that api_refusal_category describes (the banner keeps first-hop category semantics for display). Re-arm evidence for the CLI's cyber-exclusion header on session restore; never rendered, not part of the public SDK contract. Absent on cyber-free episodes and when emitted by an older CLI.

@internal Present when THIS instance was being skipped as away (two forwarded runs went unanswered in a row) until this registration cleared it: the ISO 8601 UTC instant the worker stopped asking it. Absent for a first registration, a device that was never away, and a registration that displaces a different device.
@internal Present when a newer edit from the same client came in first: this one was never raised, and its own box is echoed with no runs.

@internal Present while a mod may change what is recorded of a typed line (a hook on `prompt.submit`, `command.run`, `session.append` or, for a line sent to the session, `session.receive`; mods not yet known; or an organization policy that lists a plugin or cannot be read): what the `prompts_screened_v1` capability says on `system/init`, said as soon as a plugin load or reload makes it so. Absent says nothing: the next `system/init` does.

@internal Present, and always true, on a hand-back that auto mode's review blocked, or that it could not judge because a safety filter refused the review request: the report was delivered all the same, under the SECURITY WARNING that `handbackNote` carries. Never cap or fold such a message: show the note and the report in full. Absent on a hand-back that was not flagged, including one delivered under the note that the review was unavailable.

@internal Present, and always true, when the message is a subagent's final report to the agent that launched it, delivered through the SubagentHandback tool. Stamped by the harness, never from tool input. `body` is then the hand-back frame line with the indented report under it, and any harness note above it; `handbackReportText` and `handbackNote` carry those two parts for display. A boolean mark: not the `handback` state string of a task notification or of an Agent tool result. A hand-back is never joined, so neither this mark nor `flagged` appears beside `members`.

@internal Present, and true, only on a worker that rebuilt the conversation from the session's stored transcript before it read any request, and would not have started without it. A client may send this worker again a turn_handoff request that an earlier worker accepted, if the request names no calls (tool_use_ids empty), is not stopped, and its messages hold no tool call. A request whose turn had not ended when an earlier worker with this key stopped is left unacknowledged, so the session service sends it to this worker by itself; a second request for the same turn is answered "duplicate" while the first waits or runs. The worker appends only the messages of the turn that its conversation lacks and, once the store has confirmed every message of the turn, sends the turn's last message back as an assistant event (the echo); a turn it already holds whole is echoed on the same condition. The request can still be accepted, or refused ("invalid_handoff:"), with no echo, and the turn may then not be stored. That happens, for example, when the conversation has moved on past the part of the turn it holds, when a rewind has removed the turn, when a compaction has summarised part of it (or all of it, if the compaction was this worker's own), when a Stop clears the queue first, or when the store does not confirm the messages. A request sent again waits again for messages not yet confirmed. When a delivery finds that the store refused a message of the turn, it sends no echo and removes the turn from the conversation, and the same request sent again to that worker gets no echo. If another row has followed the turn, the turn stays, also with no echo. Exception: after 512 later refused rows the worker forgets a refusal and reads the message as confirmed. Confirmed means that the store answered the upload with success. A turn that an earlier worker's compaction summarised whole is appended a second time. The key promises nothing for a turn that holds a tool call, or whose first message is stored with no answer but with another row behind it (a hook's output, say): the worker may already have continued such a turn itself when it started. A worker without the key may have started with none of the turn's messages.

@internal Read only beside send_now:true: the uuid of the user message that Send now was pressed on, in the very form in which that message reached the CLI (a session service may deliver it in lower case): it is compared as an exact string, as cancel_async_message compares. With it only that message counts as waiting. If the running turn has already taken it in or was started for it, or the CLI does not know it or does not count it as a person's, the request does nothing and answers 'nothing_waiting', whatever else waits. Once the request acts, it acts as without the name: everything queued decides between the move to the background and the abort, and goes along with the named message. An empty string is read as no name, and so is a null, which this schema does not admit but an encoder may write; any other value that is no string names nothing.

@internal Read the session's current plan-mode plan. Unlike read_file, the caller does not need to know the plan file's path — the worker resolves its own plan slug. Never creates a plan slug or file.

@internal Registers this device's hooks with the worker — unrelated to device registration or bind. Sent by a claude --cloud device client after it attaches to a cloud session (never as an initial event of the create): names, by opaque id, which of the user's own hooks the worker should ask this device to run over hook_callback, and which vetted templates to run in the container. The worker rejects requests over 64 KiB with invalid_registration. Error replies use the standard error response with a message that starts with a code token and a colon: hook_forwarding_disabled (off for this session; not retryable, nothing stored), hook_forwarding_not_ready (retry after a short backoff), invalid_registration, or stale_worker_epoch (re-read the worker epoch and re-send). A worker that predates the request answers with the usual unsupported-subtype error.

@internal Replaces the custom system prompt (the --system-prompt / initialize systemPrompt slot). The session keeps sending the system prompt it has recorded, so the new text is first sent after the next compaction; under systemPromptSnapshot: false it is sent from the next turn on. The tool definitions already sent do not change. Applied only when the model request is accepted; must be non-empty (there is no revert-to-built-in form); re-send the current model for a prompt-only update; sending the text already in effect changes nothing. The CLAUDE_CODE_SYSTEM_PROMPT_FEATURE_FLAG per-turn read, where configured, still wins. Transports that do not implement it, and older builds, ack success without applying it.

@internal Requests one page of the stored transcript of a cloud session that the signed-in account owns. Not always the whole transcript: for a compacted session the service serves the rows its last compaction kept, then its compact_boundary entry and what followed, so the messages that compaction summarized can be on no page. Refused where list_cloud_sessions is.

@internal Resident memory of the CLI process at turn start, in whole MiB, as its kernel counts it (VmRSS in /proc/self/status). From the process's second turn on, it shows what stayed resident through the idle time since the turn before. Child processes, such as a command a tool runs or an MCP server, are left out. On a virtual machine it is the guest kernel's count, not what the host holds for the machine. Sent only by a worker that Anthropic hosts (never by a self-hosted runner, a BYOC environment, a session that Claude Desktop starts or a local run), and only with telemetry on. On such a worker it is present, always with process_rss_mib_result, where time_to_request_phases_ms is, on Linux (not WSL), unless /proc/self/status cannot be read or lacks VmRSS, or the session runs in claude-code-server.
